check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self to the mother, confirms the child's name and age, and keeps the child calm on the mother's lap with minimal handling.
Uses plain language, acknowledges the mother's fear and explains what they are doing.
History
Characterises the illness:

kids.x: Coryza for 2 days, then barking cough and noisy breathing from this evening
Noisy breathing at rest, not only when upset
Fever and how unwell the child seems

check.x: Screens for red flags of other causes:

kids.x: A sudden choking episode or something put in the mouth (inhaled foreign body)
Rash, facial or lip swelling, new food or medicine (anaphylaxis)

check.x: Asks about intake and output: drinking, eating and wet nappies.
Past history: previous croup or stridor, prematurity or airway problems, and immunisation status including Hib.
Medicines, allergies, sick contacts and who is at home.
Explores the mother's ideas, concerns and expectations.
Examination
Observes from a distance without upsetting the child:

kids.x: Inspiratory stridor at rest and barking cough
No drooling, tripod posture or cyanosis

check.x: Assesses work of breathing: respiratory rate, suprasternal and subcostal recession, tracheal tug.
Asks for SpO2, heart rate, capillary refill and temperature.
Does not examine the throat or lie the child flat, and says why (it can precipitate complete obstruction).
Listens to the chest and checks hydration.
Interpretation
Classifies the croup on arrival as moderate: stridor at rest, mild to moderate recession, not agitated, SpO2 95%.
Recognises progression to severe croup on reassessment: agitation, marked recession, tachycardia and SpO2 91%.
Considers epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, inhaled foreign body and anaphylaxis, and states the features that argue against each here.
States that croup is a clinical diagnosis and that bloods and X-rays are not routinely needed and would distress the child.
Management
On arrival: dexamethasone 0.3 mg/kg orally = 3.6 mg for 12 kg (moderate croup), as a single early dose.
Now: calls the senior doctor and ICU or anaesthetics early for severe croup.
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.5 mL/kg (6 mL calculated), capped at the 5 mL maximum, so 5 mL for 12 kg; repeats if needed with senior review.
Oxygen for SpO2 below 92%, aiming for 92% or above, given without upsetting the child (held near the face or by nasal prongs on the mother's lap).
Reassesses after adrenaline and admits for observation with continuous SpO2 for at least 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose, as stridor can return.
Explains to the mother that croup is a viral swelling of the upper airway, why the steroid and the adrenaline are given, and that the child will stay in hospital tonight.
Safety netting
Discharge only when there is no stridor at rest and no recession, at least 4 hours after the last adrenaline, the child is drinking well and the mother is confident.
Tells the mother to call 000 or return straight away for noisy breathing at rest, hard or fast breathing, drooling, blue lips, not drinking, or a drowsy child.
Arranges follow-up: GP review if the cough lasts beyond 3 to 5 days or croup keeps recurring, with written information.

desc: This station involves a focused history from the mother and a gentle examination of a 2-year-old with a barking cough and stridor, then interpreting the observations on arrival and on reassessment, classifying the croup, outlining management with weight-based doses, and safety-netting the mother.
explain:
Severity and steroid dosing

The RCH CPG classifies croup by severity. Mild croup has a barking cough with no stridor at rest. Moderate croup has stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession and little agitation. Severe croup has marked recession, agitation or lethargy, and possible hypoxia. Dexamethasone is dosed by severity: 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild, 0.3 mg/kg orally for moderate (3.6 mg for 12 kg) and 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup (7.2 mg for 12 kg), as a single dose given early. Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg is an alternative.

Interpreting the reassessment

Steroids take hours to work, so a child with moderate croup can progress to severe croup. Agitation, marked recession, a rising heart and respiratory rate and SpO2 below 92% mark severe croup and should trigger nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.5 mL/kg (maximum 5 mL; 5 mL for this 12 kg child), oxygen to target SpO2 92% or above, and early senior and ICU involvement. Adrenaline effects wear off, so observe for at least 4 hours after the last dose.

History, examination and investigations

Croup is a clinical diagnosis. The history screens for its dangerous mimics: drooling and a toxic child (epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis), a sudden choking episode (foreign body) and allergic features (anaphylaxis). Examine from a distance, keep the child on the parent's lap and do not examine the throat. Bloods and X-rays are not routinely needed and distress the child, which worsens the obstruction.

Disposition and safety netting

Children needing adrenaline are admitted, and can go home only once they have no stridor at rest, at least 4 hours have passed since the last adrenaline and they are feeding well. Parents should return urgently or call 000 for stridor at rest, increased work of breathing, drooling, cyanosis, inability to drink or lethargy.
focus: Croup in a toddler with stridor
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. A high-performing candidate takes a focused history that rules out the dangerous mimics, keeps the child calm, avoids the throat, classifies moderate croup on arrival, recognises severe croup on reassessment, gives weight-based doses correctly (dexamethasone 0.3 mg/kg = 3.6 mg; nebulised adrenaline 0.5 mL/kg capped at 5 mL), calls for senior help and gives specific discharge criteria and red flags.

A borderline candidate identifies croup but miscalculates a dose, delays escalation, or gives vague safety netting such as "come back if worse".
patient:
Role: You are the mother of a 2-year-old (12 kg). You are worried and tired. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. If the candidate tries to look in the throat or lie the child down, say the child is screaming and the noisy breathing is much worse.

Opening line: "Their breathing sounds terrible, like a seal barking, and it is getting worse."

History (give only when asked):

  • Runny nose and mild fever for 2 days. The barking cough and noisy breathing started at about 8 pm and are worse when the child cries or is upset.
  • The noisy breathing is there even when the child is sitting quietly on your lap now.
  • Highest temperature at home 38 °C. Not floppy, still interacting with you.
  • Drinking smaller amounts than usual, about half; 2 wet nappies today. Has eaten a little.
  • No drooling, swallowing normally. No choking episode, no small toys or food missing, nothing put in the mouth before it started.
  • Hoarse cry. No rash, no swelling of lips or face, no new foods or medicines.
  • No previous episodes like this. Born at term, no breathing problems as a baby, no hospital admissions.
  • Fully immunised, including the 18-month vaccines. No regular medicines. No allergies.
  • Older sibling at childcare had a cold last week. Lives with both parents, no smokers at home.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it might be asthma, like your nephew. You are scared the child will stop breathing tonight. You hope for medicine and to go home.

Questions to ask if there is time: "Is this serious?" "Why can't you look in the throat?"
points: Moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.3 mg/kg orally (3.6 mg for 12 kg) as a single early dose; mild croup is 0.15 mg/kg and severe croup is 0.6 mg/kg.
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 is 0.5 mL/kg (maximum 5 mL), so 5 mL for 12 kg; get senior and ICU help early.
Give oxygen for SpO2 below 92% and aim for 92% or above.
Observe for at least 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose; discharge needs no stridor at rest.
Keep the child calm; avoid throat examination, bloods and X-rays in typical croup.
stem: You are the junior doctor in a metropolitan Emergency Department at night. A 2-year-old child weighing 12 kg has been brought in by their mother with a runny nose for 2 days and, since this evening, a barking cough and noisy breathing. The child is sitting on the mother's lap. A nurse is with you.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother and perform a focused examination of the child, telling the examiner what you are examining and why. Keep the child calm (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the child's observations on arrival and on reassessment. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, with doses for this child, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Toddler with stridor: croup

part2.lead: Here are the observations on arrival. While you were finishing your assessment, the nurse reassessed the child 20 minutes later.

handover.label: Observations on arrival
handover.result: HR 140, RR 36, SpO2 95% on room air, CRT 2 seconds, BP 95/60, temperature 37.8 °C, AVPU alert. Inspiratory stridor at rest, mild to moderate suprasternal and subcostal recession, quiet and consolable on the mother's lap.

handover.label: Reassessment 20 minutes later
handover.result: Agitated and difficult to settle, loud stridor at rest, marked recession with tracheal tug. RR 52, HR 170, SpO2 91% on room air. No drooling.

handover.label: Investigations
handover.result: None done. If requested, the examiner says bloods and a neck or chest X-ray are not indicated and would distress the child.

ask: How would you classify this child's croup on arrival, and on reassessment?
What else would you consider, and what would point to it?
What is your management on arrival and now? Give drugs with doses for this child.
When could this child go home, and what would you tell the mother to watch for?
